content: Acquired antithrombin (AT) deficiency is a frequently observed and clinically significant condition in preterm infants suffering from respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). It has been proposed that administering AT concentrate might improve clinical outcomes in these infants. To evaluate this hypothesis, a systematic review was conducted to assess the effects of AT concentrate compared to placebo or no treatment on mortality in preterm infants with RDS. An extensive electronic search of databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, was performed in August 2006, with an update in December 2009. Additional sources, such as references from identified studies, unpublished data from experts and pharmaceutical companies, and abstracts from pediatric research meetings (1983–2005), were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared any dose and duration of AT therapy with placebo or no treatment in preterm infants diagnosed with RDS. Two RCTs, involving a total of 182 preterm infants, met the inclusion criteria. The mean gestational age of the infants was 28 weeks. In one trial, eligibility required infants to be intubated and ventilated for RDS, while the other trial did not explicitly list RDS as an inclusion criterion, though most infants in that study received surfactant therapy. Neither of the individual trials demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in mortality with AT treatment. Notably, one of the trials was terminated prematurely due to an observed increase in mortality in the AT treatment group. A pooled analysis of mortality within the first week of life revealed a relative risk of 2.67 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.72 to 9.83) favoring the control group, though this result was not statistically significant. Only the prematurely terminated trial followed infants long enough to report neonatal mortality rates. In this trial, 7 deaths (11.5%) occurred in the AT group compared to 2 deaths (3.3%) in the placebo group within the first 28 days of life. Secondary outcomes, such as the duration of mechanical ventilation and supplemental oxygen use, were reported in only one trial. Both outcomes significantly favored the control group, with statistically significant differences (p < 0.05). In conclusion, the evidence suggests that preterm infants with RDS are unlikely to derive benefit from AT treatment. On the contrary, AT therapy may pose potential harm, as indicated by the increased mortality observed in one of the trials.
